toc.title: The lifecycle, model sources and AWS services by stage

html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Describe the phases of the ML lifecycle and how they differ
  • Name the sources of models: open source, provider models and custom training
  • Compare managed API and self-hosted API ways to run a model
  • Match AWS services to each stage of the pipeline
  • Explain MLOps and read accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and business metrics

2The lifecycle, model sources and AWS services by stage

Running case

Cedar and Salt Plans a Cancellation Model

  • Cedar and Salt loses money on late cancellations; the team wants a cancellation-risk model
  • Before any code, leaders ask: what are the steps, where does the model come from, and how will we run it?
  • They also ask how we will know it is good, in model terms and in money terms
  • Your job: walk the team through the lifecycle, services, MLOps and metrics

The ML Lifecycle at a Glance

  • 1 Business goal: the problem and the value to gain
  • 2 Problem framing: turn it into an ML problem with a target to predict
  • 3 Data processing: collect, prepare and engineer features
  • 4 Model development: train, tune and evaluate
  • 5 Deployment: make predictions in production
  • 6 Monitoring: check performance over time, then loop back

Exam tip: The phases are a cycle, not a straight line: monitoring feeds new data and retraining.

Business Goal and Problem Framing

  • Business goal: state the problem and the value to be gained, with measurable success criteria
  • Problem framing: say what is observed and what should be predicted (the label or target)
  • Decide how performance and error will be measured
  • Check first that ML is the right tool (Module 2)
  • Cedar and Salt: predict whether a booking will be canceled, to cut empty rooms

Exam tip: Starting with the business goal is the first step; data and models come later.

Data Processing: Collect, Prepare and Engineer Features

  • Collect data from many sources into one place, often Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3)
  • Prepare it: clean errors, fix inconsistent values, handle missing data
  • Engineer features: create, transform and select the variables the model learns from
  • Data quality sets the ceiling for model quality
  • Split the data: most to train, the rest to validate and test

Exam tip: Poor data gives a poor model, however good the algorithm.

Model Development: Train, Tune and Evaluate

  • Train: an algorithm learns from the training data to produce a model
  • Tune: adjust settings (hyperparameters) to improve results; done by specialists, not tested in depth
  • Evaluate: measure quality on data the model has not seen, with metrics
  • A CI/CD pipeline can automate build, train and release
  • Training can start from an algorithm or a pre-trained base model

Exam tip: Always evaluate on data the model did not train on.

Deployment and Monitoring

  • Deploy the model so applications can request inferences
  • Monitor it: performance can degrade as the world changes
  • Drift means the data or the relationship it learned has shifted
  • When quality drops, collect new data and retrain
  • Cedar and Salt: travel patterns change by season, so the model must be watched

Exam tip: Deployment is not the end: a model needs monitoring and retraining.

Where Models Come From [Verify live]

Source What it means On AWS
Open-source pre-trained models Publicly available models you can use, adapt or fine-tune SageMaker JumpStart model hub
Provider models Foundation models from AWS and other companies, used through an API Amazon Bedrock, with Amazon and other providers
Custom-trained models You train a model on your own data SageMaker AI
  • As of 5 November 2026: Bedrock lists 100+ models from providers including Amazon, Anthropic, DeepSeek, OpenAI and xAI

Exam tip: Starting from a pre-trained model is faster and cheaper than training from scratch.

Ways to Use a Model in Production

Method How it works Trade-off
Managed API service AWS runs the model and scales it; you call an API (Amazon Bedrock, SageMaker AI endpoints) Less work, less control
Self-hosted API You run the model on your own compute, such as Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2), ECS or EKS, and expose your own API More control, more to operate
  • Choose managed to move fast with a small team; choose self-hosted for custom runtimes or special control needs

Exam tip: No servers to manage: managed API service. Full control of the stack: self-hosted API.

AWS Services by Stage of the Pipeline

Stage AWS services and features
Data Amazon S3, AWS Glue, Glue DataBrew (no-code cleaning), AWS Data Exchange (third-party data), Amazon EMR, Amazon Redshift
Build and train Amazon SageMaker AI, Amazon Bedrock; Kiro, an AI-powered development environment, to write the application code
Deploy SageMaker AI endpoints, Amazon Bedrock; Amazon EC2, ECS or EKS for self-hosting
Use the results Amazon Quick, an AI companion for research, business insights and automation
Monitor SageMaker Model Monitor, Amazon CloudWatch

Exam tip: Match the stage to the service: data prep, build, deploy, use, monitor.

3MLOps, metrics and practice

MLOps: What and Why

  • MLOps applies DevOps ideas to ML so models reach production reliably
  • Experimentation: try and track many versions
  • Repeatable processes: automate pipelines instead of one-off notebooks
  • Scalable systems: handle more data and requests
  • Managing technical debt and production readiness
  • Model monitoring and re-training when performance drops

Exam tip: MLOps is about repeatable, monitored delivery of models, not a single tool.

MLOps on Amazon SageMaker AI

Need SageMaker AI capability
Track and compare experiments SageMaker Experiments
Automate the workflow SageMaker AI Workflows (Pipelines)
Version and approve models Model Registry
Follow what produced a model ML Lineage Tracking
Watch a live model Model Monitor
Set up CI/CD for ML SageMaker Projects

Exam tip: Version a model: Model Registry. Watch it in production: Model Monitor.

Model Performance Metrics

Metric Meaning Think
Accuracy Correct predictions out of all predictions Overall hit rate
Precision Of the items predicted positive, how many really are Few false alarms
Recall Of the real positives, how many were found Few misses
F1 score The balance of precision and recall One combined score
  • AUC summarizes how well a classifier separates classes across thresholds Beyond the guide

Exam tip: Precision cares about false positives; recall cares about false negatives.

Precision or Recall?

Situation Costly mistake Favor
Flag every booking likely to cancel A miss (false negative) Recall
Send a costly retention offer only to real risks A false alarm (false positive) Precision
Keep both in balance Either mistake F1 score
A dataset where one class is rare Accuracy can mislead Precision, recall or F1

Exam tip: Accuracy alone can hide problems when one class is rare.

Business Metrics for an ML Model

  • A model can score well and still not pay off: measure business value too
  • Cost per user or per prediction
  • Development costs and running costs
  • Customer feedback and satisfaction
  • Return on investment (ROI)
  • Compare the model's value with the cost to build and run it

Exam tip: F1 and accuracy are model metrics; ROI and cost per user are business metrics.

What the Exam Asks: The Lifecycle, MLOps and Metrics

  • Which phase: business goal, framing, data processing, model development, deployment or monitoring
  • Which source: open-source pre-trained, provider model or custom-trained
  • Which way to run: managed API service or self-hosted API
  • Which service: S3, Glue DataBrew, Data Exchange, SageMaker AI, Bedrock, Model Monitor
  • Which MLOps idea: repeatable, scalable, monitored, retrained
  • Which metric: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 or a business metric

Exam tip: Name the phase or the need first, then the service or metric.

Design Check: Cedar and Salt's Cancellation Model

Step in order Phase
1 Cut empty rooms from late cancellations Business goal
2 Predict canceled or not Problem framing
3 Clean and prepare past bookings Data processing
4 Train and evaluate with F1 Model development
5 Call it from the booking site Deployment
6 Watch for seasonal drift, retrain Monitoring
  • Match a metric to each worry: missed cancellations need recall; wasted offers need precision; payback needs ROI

4Exam Q&A

4.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1Which sequence lists the phases of the ML lifecycle in the correct order?

  • AData processing, business goal, problem framing, model development, deployment, monitoring
  • BProblem framing, business goal, data processing, deployment, model development, monitoring
  • CBusiness goal, data processing, problem framing, model development, monitoring, deployment
  • DBusiness goal, problem framing, data processing, model development, deployment, monitoring
Show the answer

Answer: D. The lifecycle starts with the business goal, then frames the problem, processes the data, develops the model, deploys it and monitors it, with feedback loops back to earlier phases.

S2Cedar and Salt's small team wants its booking site to call the cancellation model through an API, without managing servers or scaling. Which approach fits best?

  • AHost the model in a self-hosted API on its own Amazon EC2 fleet
  • BUse a managed API service, such as a SageMaker AI endpoint
  • CRun the model inside a spreadsheet macro
  • DRetrain the model on every request
Show the answer

Answer: B. A managed API service runs and scales the model for you, so the team calls an API and manages no servers. A self-hosted API gives more control but means running and scaling the compute yourself.

S3Which TWO are fundamental MLOps concepts? (Select TWO.)

  • ARepeatable, automated processes instead of one-off steps
  • BMonitoring a model and re-training it when performance drops
  • CTraining a model once and never checking it again
  • DKeeping each experiment undocumented
  • EIgnoring technical debt until the model fails
Show the answer

Answer: A, B. MLOps stresses repeatable, automated processes, experimentation tracking, scalable systems, managing technical debt, and monitoring with re-training. The other options describe habits MLOps tries to remove.

S4Missing a booking that will actually be canceled is very costly, so the team wants to find as many real cancellations as possible. Which metric should it favor?

  • ARecall, the share of real positives that are found
  • BPrecision, the share of predicted positives that are real
  • CMean squared error, which measures numeric prediction error
  • DLatency, which measures response time
Show the answer

Answer: A. Recall measures how many of the real positives the model finds, so it is the metric to favor when misses are costly. Precision penalizes false alarms, and the other options do not measure classification quality.

S5An analyst with no coding skills wants to clean and normalize raw booking data visually before it is used for ML. Which AWS service fits?

  • AAWS Data Exchange
  • BAmazon Rekognition
  • CAWS Glue DataBrew
  • DAmazon Polly
Show the answer

Answer: C. AWS Glue DataBrew is a visual data preparation tool that cleans and normalizes data without code. Data Exchange finds third-party data, Rekognition analyzes images, and Polly turns text into speech.

S6Which of the following is a business metric for evaluating an ML model, rather than a model performance metric?

  • AF1 score, the balance of precision and recall
  • BPrecision, the share of positive predictions that are correct
  • CRecall, the share of actual positives that are found
  • DReturn on investment (ROI)
Show the answer

Answer: D. ROI compares the value an ML solution brings with its cost, so it is a business metric. F1 score, precision and recall measure how well a model predicts.

5Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Lifecycle business goal, problem framing, data processing, model development, deployment, monitoring
Models come from open-source pre-trained, provider models and custom training
Run a model a managed API service or a self-hosted API
MLOps experimentation, repeatable and scalable processes, monitoring and retraining
Metrics accuracy, precision, recall and F1, plus business metrics such as ROI
